newsitem.title: PERU: After Peru crisis, embassies shelve parties.
newsitem.headline: After Peru crisis, embassies shelve parties.

text.p: The pop of champagne corks and the strains of piano music as VIPs socialize at glitzy embassy receptions are rare occurrences these days, fallout from the four-month hostage siege at the Japanese ambassador's home.

The Marxist rebels' storming of a party that was one of the high points on the diplomatic social calendar -- a reception to honour Japan's Emperor Akihito -- has traumatized Lima's elite and led embassies to scale back such functions.
"I don't want to sit through four months with terrorists," one former regular of the Lima cocktail party circuit, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.

The Dec. 17 reception at Tokyo's luxurious diplomatic mansion turned into a nightmare when a band of gun-toting Tupac Amaru rebels blew their way in to take more than 500 hostages including ambassadors, ministers, top security officials and relatives of President Alberto Fujimori.
The group held on to 72 of their most valuable captives in cramped and dirty conditions until the April 22 military strike that killed the 14 rebels and safely freed all but one of the hostages.
"It was the longest cocktail party I've ever had," said Japan's shell-shocked ambassador, Morihisa Aoki.

The head of security at the Swedish embassy in Lima said diplomatic functions in the capital with more than about 50 people had been largely shelved due to safety fears. The Swedish Embassy has cancelled its June 6 national celebration.
"We have not even planned it. We know it's not possible to have it under these difficulties. It would feel uncomfortable ...like going to a funeral," the Swedish official said.
He added that any large function would need police both outside and inside, which diplomats do not like.

The few receptions still on the social calendar are often held in rented locations, rather than the customary settings of plush embassies or ambassadors' homes. Most are now held during the day and with smaller numbers invited.

The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's (MRTA) 126-day takeover underscored the lax security in protecting embassies from attacks by guerrillas in this South American nation. Nineteen senior police officers are on trial for the security lapse that allowed the takeover.
"If you're well-dressed you can practically get in anywhere," said one regular at Lima diplomatic functions, adding that she and friends had often entered receptions without invitations.
The Swedish official said security had improved since the hostage crisis, but was still erratic.

"It's very varied," he said. "Some days two men stand outside the embassy with different weapons -- sometimes with machine guns, at other times with only small guns. Sometimes there is only one, at other times no one".
A few embassies, however, have declined to change their protocol.
"We are holding our functions as planned," said a British embassy spokeswoman, adding that "we just held the Queen's birthday celebration on April 21".
And a U.S. embassy official said: "It's business as usual for us," but added "we have beefed up security around the embassy and the residence."
The U.S. embassy, considered the most secure in Peru and nicknamed "the bunker", will proceed with its most important annual event, the Fourth of July or Independence Day party, he said.
But the British and U.S. embassies' official bravado contrasted with the feeling among individual diplomats and party-goers.
"Since the hostage crisis the atmosphere has changed," said one young socialite. "You can count the parties on your fingers."
The latest high-profile casualty on the party circuit was the Netherlands' cancellation of the April 30 Queen's Day celebration.

Israel plans to go ahead with its imminent national celebration, but will move the party to the high-security Museum of the Nation and have guests arrive at intervals to reduce risks, according to diplomatic sources.
"For Israel's national day celebrations last year over 1,000 people went. This year only 400 are expected," said prominent businessman and reception regular Jorge Gruenberg.
